subject: biology

questions.content: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. Veins carry blood back to the heart.

questions.content: Which part of the blood carries oxygen?
questions.explanation: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds to oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues.

questions.content: How many chambers does the human heart have?
questions.explanation: The heart has two atria (upper) and two ventricles (lower).

questions.content: What is the function of platelets?
questions.explanation: Platelets are cell fragments that help blood clot at a wound, sealing it and stopping bleeding.

questions.content: Why do veins have valves?
questions.explanation: Blood in veins is at low pressure, so valves prevent backflow and keep blood moving towards the heart.

questions.content: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

questions.content: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than the right ventricle?
options: It pumps blood around the whole body at higher pressure
It pumps blood to the lungs only
questions.explanation: The left ventricle sends blood to the body through the aorta, which needs high pressure. The right pumps to the nearby lungs.

questions.content: Why is the circulation in humans described as a double circulation?
options: Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit
questions.explanation: Blood goes from the heart to the lungs and back, then from the heart to the body and back, passing through the heart twice per circuit.

questions.content: Which feature makes capillaries well suited to exchanging substances?
questions.explanation: Thin walls give a short diffusion distance for oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide between blood and cells.

questions.content: A person's heart beats 72 times a minute and pumps 70 mL of blood with each beat. What is the volume pumped per minute?
questions.explanation: 72 × 70 = 5 040 mL per minute.

questions.content: Which cells are mainly responsible for making antibodies?
questions.explanation: Lymphocytes are white blood cells that make antibodies. Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens.

questions.content: A student feels her pulse at the wrist at 80 beats per minute while resting and 130 after a run. What is the best explanation?
options: Muscles need more oxygen and glucose, so the heart beats faster
There is less blood in the body
questions.explanation: Exercise raises the energy demand, so heart rate rises to deliver more oxygen and glucose and remove carbon dioxide.

questions.content: Which statement about arteries is correct?
options: They have valves to stop backflow
They have thick elastic walls to withstand high pressure
They have walls one cell thick
questions.explanation: Arteries have thick elastic and muscular walls. The pulmonary artery is an exception that carries deoxygenated blood.

questions.content: A blocked coronary artery leads to a heart attack. Why does this damage the heart muscle?
options: The blood has too many platelets
The heart muscle has too much oxygen
The muscle cells lose their oxygen and glucose supply and cannot respire
questions.explanation: Coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself. If blocked, the cells starve of oxygen and glucose and die.

questions.content: A sprinter's resting heart rate is 60 beats per minute with a stroke volume of 90 mL. Calculate the cardiac output in mL per minute.
questions.explanation: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 60 × 90 = 5 400 mL per minute.

questions.content: Blood pressure is highest in arteries, lower in capillaries and lowest in veins. Which statement explains why valves are needed in veins but not arteries?
options: Blood in veins has low pressure so cannot be pushed back by the heart alone
questions.explanation: Arterial blood is pushed on by the pulse from the heart, but vein blood relies on muscle squeezing, so valves stop backflow.

questions.content: A patient has a hole between the left and right ventricles, so some oxygenated blood mixes with deoxygenated blood. What is the likely effect?
options: More oxygen is delivered to the tissues
Less oxygen is delivered to the body tissues
No effect because the blood is the same
questions.explanation: Mixing reduces the oxygen content of the blood sent around the body, so cells get less oxygen for respiration.

questions.content: A doctor tests how well a drug lowers heart rate. Patients are given the drug and heart rates are measured before and after. What is the best way to make the results more reliable?
options: Give the drug to everyone and ignore other factors
Use a larger group and include a control group not given the drug
questions.explanation: A larger sample reduces the effect of chance, and a control group lets the effect of the drug be separated from other causes.

note:
The circulatory system
Your body is made of trillions of cells that need a constant supply of oxygen and glucose and a way to remove waste such as carbon dioxide. The circulatory system does this job. It has three main parts: the heart (the pump), the blood vessels (the pipes) and the blood (the transport fluid). Humans have a **double circulation**: blood passes through the heart twice on each complete circuit of the body. One loop goes to the lungs to pick up oxygen, and the other goes to the rest of the body.

## The heart
The heart is made of cardiac muscle and has four chambers.
- The **right atrium** receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava.
- The **right ventricle** pumps it to the lungs through the pulmonary artery.
- The **left atrium** receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary vein.
- The **left ventricle** pumps it around the body through the aorta.

The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right because it pumps blood a long way at higher pressure. Valves between the atria and ventricles, and at the exits, keep the blood flowing in one direction. The heart muscle has its own blood supply from the **coronary arteries**. If one is blocked, the muscle is starved of oxygen and a heart attack may occur. Cardiac output is the volume pumped per minute: heart rate × stroke volume. For example, 72 beats per minute × 70 mL = 5 040 mL per minute.

## Blood vessels
- **Arteries** carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. They have thick, elastic, muscular walls and a narrow lumen.
- **Veins** carry blood towards the heart at low pressure. They have thinner walls, a wider lumen and valves to prevent backflow.
- **Capillaries** are tiny vessels with walls one cell thick. They form networks around the tissues, so substances can diffuse quickly between the blood and cells.

A common trap is to say arteries always carry oxygenated blood. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood. The correct rule is: arteries away, veins towards.

## Blood
Blood has four main components:
- **Plasma**: a pale yellow liquid that carries dissolved glucose, carbon dioxide, hormones, urea and heat.
- **Red blood cells**: carry oxygen using haemoglobin. They are biconcave discs with no nucleus, giving a large surface area and more room for haemoglobin.
- **White blood cells**: defend against disease. Phagocytes engulf pathogens and lymphocytes make antibodies.
- **Platelets**: fragments of cells that help blood clot.

## Heart rate and exercise
During exercise muscle cells respire faster. The heart rate rises to deliver more oxygen and glucose and to remove carbon dioxide. Regular exercise strengthens the heart, so the resting heart rate is often lower. Diet, smoking and stress can affect heart health. Fatty deposits in the coronary arteries can narrow them and lead to coronary heart disease.

## Common mistakes
- Mixing up artery and vein. Remember: arteries carry blood Away.
- Saying the left side of the heart is on the left of the page. In diagrams the heart is drawn as if seen from the front, so the left side appears on the right.
- Saying blood is "used up". Blood circulates and is reused.

## How this is examined
You may be given a diagram of the heart to label, a table of heart rates before and after exercise, or a scenario about a patient. Expect calculations (cardiac output, percentage change), explanations linking structure to function, and evaluations of how reliable an investigation is.

Exam tip: To explain a structure-and-function question, give the feature, then the effect, such as thick walls so that they withstand high pressure.

flashcards.back: Blood passes through the heart twice per circuit: heart → lungs → heart → body.
Right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; veins carry blood towards the heart at low pressure and have valves.
Walls one cell thick for quick diffusion of oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide.
Carry oxygen using haemoglobin. Biconcave and no nucleus.
Phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes make antibodies.
Cell fragments that help blood clot.
Heart rate × stroke volume (volume pumped per minute).
Supply the heart muscle with oxygen and glucose. A blockage can cause a heart attack.

subject: biology

questions.content: Which is the correct path of air into the lungs?
questions.explanation: Air passes down the trachea, which divides into two bronchi, then into smaller bronchioles ending in alveoli.

questions.content: Which muscle contracts and flattens during inhalation?
questions.explanation: When the diaphragm contracts and flattens, the volume of the chest increases, drawing air in.

questions.content: What is the function of mucus in the airways?
questions.explanation: Mucus traps particles and pathogens. Cilia then sweep it up towards the throat.

questions.content: Which harmful substance in cigarette smoke is addictive?
questions.explanation: Nicotine is the addictive drug. Tar causes cancer and carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carried by the blood.

questions.content: What is the role of cilia in the trachea?
options: To move mucus and trapped particles up and away from the lungs
To push air into the lungs
questions.explanation: Cilia are tiny hairs on cells that beat to sweep mucus upwards.

questions.content: During exhalation at rest, what happens to the ribcage and diaphragm?
options: Ribs move down and in; diaphragm relaxes and rises
questions.explanation: Chest volume decreases, pressure increases above atmospheric pressure, and air is forced out.

questions.content: A person takes 15 breaths per minute, each moving 500 mL of air. What volume of air moves per minute?
questions.explanation: 15 × 500 = 7 500 mL per minute.

questions.content: Which best describes what happens in an asthma attack?
options: Airway muscles contract and the lining swells, narrowing the airways
questions.explanation: In asthma, airways narrow due to muscle tightening, swelling and extra mucus, making breathing difficult. An inhaler relaxes the muscle.

questions.content: Why does carbon monoxide in smoke reduce the oxygen carried by the blood?
options: It binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen
It makes red blood cells larger
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin, so there is less haemoglobin free to carry oxygen.

questions.content: A student measures her breathing rate sitting (14 breaths per minute) and after running (30 breaths per minute). By what percentage did it increase?
questions.explanation: (30 − 14) ÷ 14 × 100 = 114.3%. Percentage change is the increase divided by the original value.

questions.content: Which statement correctly compares inhaled and exhaled air?
options: Exhaled air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide
Exhaled air has less carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Some oxygen is absorbed and carbon dioxide is added, but exhaled air still contains about 16% oxygen.

questions.content: Why is it better to breathe in through the nose than the mouth?
options: Hairs and mucus filter, warm and moisten the air
The mouth cannot reach the trachea
questions.explanation: The nose has hairs and mucus that trap particles, and a good blood supply that warms the air.

questions.content: Which gas exchange surface is damaged by emphysema, a disease linked to smoking?
questions.explanation: Emphysema breaks down the walls of alveoli, reducing surface area and so oxygen absorption.

questions.content: Tidal volume is the amount of air in a normal breath. A student breathes 6 000 mL per minute at rest at 12 breaths per minute. What is her tidal volume?
questions.explanation: Tidal volume = volume per minute ÷ breaths per minute = 6 000 ÷ 12 = 500 mL.

questions.content: A spirometer trace shows that after exercise training a person's breathing rate at rest has dropped but oxygen intake is unchanged. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Each breath is deeper, so the same volume moves with fewer breaths
questions.explanation: If oxygen intake is the same and rate falls, then volume per breath must have risen. Training improves lung efficiency.

questions.content: Smokers' cilia are damaged and paralysed. Why does this lead to a 'smoker's cough'?
options: Mucus and trapped particles collect and must be coughed out
questions.explanation: Without working cilia, mucus builds up in the airway, and coughing is the only way to clear it, which also increases the risk of infection.

questions.content: In a study, 1 000 smokers and 1 000 non-smokers were followed for 20 years. 90 smokers and 10 non-smokers developed lung cancer. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Smoking is associated with a higher rate of lung cancer
The study proves nicotine causes cancer
questions.explanation: 9% of smokers and 1% of non-smokers developed lung cancer, so there is a strong association. The data alone cannot prove nicotine is the cause or that all cases are due to smoking.

questions.content: During a rise in altitude, a hiker's breathing rate and heart rate both increase after a few hours. Which explanation best links the two?
options: Carbon dioxide has been used up
Lower oxygen levels trigger a faster supply of oxygen to the tissues
questions.explanation: Lower air pressure gives less oxygen per breath, so the body compensates by breathing faster and circulating blood faster.

note:
The respiratory system
The respiratory system brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide. It is made up of the airways and the lungs, plus the muscles that move air. Remember that **breathing** (ventilation) is the movement of air in and out of the lungs, whereas **respiration** is the chemical reaction in cells that releases energy. Breathing supports respiration by providing oxygen and removing carbon dioxide.

## The structures
- **Nose and mouth**: air enters. The nose has hairs and mucus to trap dust and a rich blood supply to warm the air.
- **Trachea (windpipe)**: a tube held open by rings of cartilage. It is lined with ciliated cells and goblet cells that produce mucus.
- **Bronchi**: two tubes (singular bronchus), one into each lung.
- **Bronchioles**: smaller branching tubes.
- **Alveoli**: tiny air sacs surrounded by capillaries, where gas exchange takes place.
- **Ribcage, intercostal muscles and diaphragm**: move air in and out.

The lungs are protected by the ribcage and covered by moist pleural membranes that reduce friction as the lungs move.

## How breathing works
Breathing depends on changing the volume and pressure inside the chest (thorax).
- Inhaling: the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles raise the ribs. The chest volume increases, the pressure falls below the pressure of the air outside, and air flows in.
- Exhaling at rest: the diaphragm relaxes and rises into a dome, and the ribs move down and in. The chest volume decreases, the pressure rises and air is forced out.

Normal quiet breathing moves about 500 mL of air per breath (the tidal volume). Ventilation rate per minute = breaths per minute × volume per breath, for example 15 × 500 = 7 500 mL per minute. Exercise increases both the rate and the depth.

## Keeping the airways clean
The airways are lined with mucus-producing cells and cells with cilia. Mucus traps dust, pollen and microbes. The cilia beat to sweep the mucus up to the throat, where it is swallowed or coughed out. This protects the delicate alveoli.

## Problems of the respiratory system
- **Asthma**: the airways become narrow because the muscle in their walls contracts, the lining swells and more mucus is produced. Triggers include pollen, dust, exercise and cold air. A reliever inhaler relaxes the muscles so the airways widen.
- **Smoking**: tobacco smoke contains nicotine (addictive), tar (a sticky mixture that contains cancer-causing chemicals) and carbon monoxide (binds to haemoglobin and reduces oxygen transport). Smoking paralyses cilia, causes a smoker's cough and bronchitis, and can lead to emphysema (alveoli walls break down) and lung cancer. It also increases the risk of heart disease.
- **Air pollution** such as smoke, traffic fumes and particles can irritate the airways and worsen asthma.

## Interpreting data
Studies on smoking often compare groups of smokers and non-smokers. If 9% of smokers develop a disease and 1% of non-smokers do, there is a strong association. Data like this show a link but good evaluation also considers sample size, how long the study lasted and other factors such as age or diet that might have an effect.

## Common mistakes
- Saying that we breathe in only oxygen and breathe out only carbon dioxide.
- Saying the lungs push air in. In fact the lungs are passive, and the muscles change the chest volume.
- Mixing up ribs "up and out" for inhaling with exhaling.

## How this is examined
You may see a diagram of the airways, a table of breathing rates or a study of smokers and non-smokers. Expect questions on labelling, explaining how a structure helps, and evaluating evidence.

Exam tip: Describe breathing in order: muscles contract or relax, chest volume changes, pressure changes, then air moves.

flashcards.back: Nose/mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
Diaphragm contracts and flattens, ribs up and out, volume up, pressure down, air flows in.
Diaphragm relaxes and rises, ribs down and in, volume down, pressure up, air flows out.
Mucus traps dust and microbes; cilia sweep it up and away from the lungs.
Breaths per minute × volume per breath (tidal volume).
Airways narrow because of muscle contraction, swelling and mucus. Relievers relax the muscle.

flashcards.front: Three harmful substances in tobacco smoke
flashcards.back: Nicotine (addictive), tar (carcinogens), carbon monoxide (reduces oxygen carried).
Alveoli walls break down, reducing the surface area for gas exchange.
Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is the release of energy from glucose in cells.

subject: biology

questions.content: Which two organs make up the central nervous system?
questions.explanation: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord. Nerves outside it form the peripheral nervous system.

questions.content: What is a reflex action?
options: A response controlled by hormones only
A fast, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought
questions.explanation: Reflexes are rapid and automatic, which protects the body from danger.

questions.content: Which type of neurone carries impulses from receptors to the CNS?
questions.explanation: Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS. Motor neurones carry them from the CNS to effectors.

questions.content: What is an effector?
options: A cell that detects a stimulus
A muscle or gland that responds to a stimulus
questions.explanation: Effectors are muscles (which contract) or glands (which release substances).

questions.content: Which part of the brain controls balance and coordination?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance. The medulla controls automatic actions like heart rate and breathing.

questions.content: Put the reflex arc in the correct order.
options: Stimulus → effector → relay neurone → receptor → response
Receptor → motor neurone → relay neurone → sensory neurone → effector
Stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector → response
questions.explanation: The impulse passes from receptor via sensory, relay and motor neurones to the effector, which produces the response.

questions.content: Why is a reflex faster than a voluntary action?
options: The pathway is short and does not involve the conscious part of the brain
questions.explanation: In a reflex, the relay neurone is in the spinal cord, so there is no delay for conscious decision-making.

questions.content: What is a synapse?
options: A small gap between two neurones
questions.explanation: At a synapse a chemical (neurotransmitter) diffuses across the gap and starts a new impulse in the next neurone.

questions.content: A student drops a ruler and a partner catches it, 20 cm from the zero mark. Using time = √(2 × distance ÷ 9.8) with distance in metres, what is the reaction time?
In the ruler drop test, repeat trials give catch distances of 18, 22, 20 and 20 cm. What is the mean distance?
Which structure carries a nerve impulse a long way, like a cable?
questions.explanation: The axon is the long fibre of a neurone. Motor neurones have long axons covered by a fatty myelin sheath that speeds up impulses.

questions.content: Why do the pupils of the eye get smaller in bright light?
options: The pupil is controlled by thought
A reflex protects the retina from damage
questions.explanation: The iris muscles contract in bright light to reduce the amount of light entering, an automatic reflex.

questions.content: Which of these is a voluntary action?
options: Blinking when dust enters the eye
Choosing to pick up a pen
Pulling a hand from a hot object
questions.explanation: Voluntary actions are controlled consciously by the brain. The other three are reflexes.

questions.content: A person touches something hot and pulls their hand away before feeling pain. What explains this order of events?
options: The pain impulses travel faster than reflex impulses
The brain sends the response before the stimulus
The reflex arc triggers the response before the impulse reaches the conscious brain
questions.explanation: The reflex goes through the spinal cord, so the muscle responds first. Impulses also travel up to the brain, so pain is felt a moment later.

questions.content: A patient has a damaged spinal cord and cannot feel their feet, but the knee-jerk reflex still works below the injury. What does this suggest?
options: The reflex arc is intact because it does not need the brain
The sensory neurones are all destroyed
questions.explanation: The knee-jerk is a spinal reflex. Impulses to the brain are blocked by the injury, so sensation is lost, but the arc remains functional.

questions.content: In a reaction time experiment, a student's mean time is 0.25 s when alone but 0.40 s when also reading a text message. What is the percentage increase?
questions.explanation: (0.40 − 0.25) ÷ 0.25 × 100 = 60%. Distraction slows the reaction, which is important for road safety.

questions.content: A drug blocks the receptors on the receiving neurone of a synapse. What is the most likely effect?
options: Impulses cannot pass across the synapse
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitter molecules must bind to receptors to start a new impulse. If blocked, transmission stops.

questions.content: A researcher tests whether caffeine affects reaction time using 5 volunteers, each tested once with a drink containing caffeine and once without. Which improvement would make the conclusions most reliable?
options: Repeat each test several times with more volunteers and in random order
questions.explanation: More participants and repeats reduce chance effects, and random order stops practice effects from affecting the results.

note:
The nervous system
The nervous system lets you detect changes in the world around you and respond quickly. It is made of the **central nervous system (CNS)**, the brain and the spinal cord, and the **peripheral nervous system**, the nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body. Information travels along nerve cells (neurones) as tiny electrical signals called **impulses**.

## Neurones
There are three types of neurone.
- **Sensory neurones** carry impulses from receptors to the CNS.
- **Relay neurones** are in the CNS and connect sensory and motor neurones.
- **Motor neurones** carry impulses from the CNS to effectors.

A neurone has a cell body, branched dendrites that receive signals and a long **axon** that carries the impulse. Many axons are covered by a fatty myelin sheath, which speeds up impulses. Neurones do not touch. At a **synapse**, a tiny gap, the impulse triggers the release of a chemical neurotransmitter that diffuses across the gap and binds to receptors on the next neurone, starting a new impulse. Synapses make sure that impulses only travel in one direction.

## Stimulus and response
A **stimulus** is a change in the environment, such as heat, light or pressure. **Receptors** detect stimuli. The CNS is the coordinator, and **effectors**, which are muscles or glands, carry out the response. The general sequence is: stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response.

## Reflex actions
A **reflex** is a fast, automatic, protective response that does not need conscious thought. Examples include pulling your hand away from a hot object, blinking and the pupil getting smaller in bright light. The reflex arc is:
stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in the spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector → response.
Because the relay neurone is in the spinal cord, the message does not have to go to the conscious part of the brain, which saves time. Impulses also pass up to the brain, so you notice what happened a moment later.

## The brain
- **Cerebrum**: the largest part, responsible for thought, memory, language and conscious actions, and receiving information from the senses.
- **Cerebellum**: coordinates movement and balance.
- **Medulla**: controls automatic actions, such as heart rate and breathing.

## Investigating reaction time
A popular test is the ruler drop. One person holds a ruler vertically and the partner catches it. The distance dropped is converted into time using time = √(2 × distance ÷ 9.8), with distance in metres. For 20 cm (0.20 m) the time is about 0.20 s. Good practice: repeat several trials and take a mean, use the same hand, and test for factors such as caffeine, practice or distraction one at a time. A shorter distance caught means a faster reaction.

## Common mistakes
- Saying hormones control reflexes. Reflexes are nervous.
- Mixing up sensory and motor neurones. Sensory = into the CNS; motor = out.
- Saying reflexes bypass the brain entirely. The brain is bypassed for the response, but not for sensation.
- Forgetting to mention the effector.

## How this is examined
Expect a reflex-arc flow chart, reaction time data with mean and percentage change, or a scenario involving injury, drugs or distraction. Evaluating fair tests and reliability is a regular feature.

Exam tip: When asked why a reflex is fast, mention a short pathway through the spinal cord, no conscious decision and a protective purpose.

Sensory: receptor to CNS. Relay: inside CNS. Motor: CNS to effector.
Stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector → response.
A fast, automatic, protective response without conscious thought.
A gap between neurones. A neurotransmitter diffuses across to start a new impulse.
A muscle or a gland that carries out the response.
Cerebrum: thought and memory. Cerebellum: balance and coordination. Medulla: heart rate and breathing.
Pulling a hand from heat, blinking, pupil narrowing in bright light.

subject: biology

questions.content: What is a hormone?
options: An electrical signal in a neurone
A chemical messenger made in a gland and carried in the blood
questions.explanation: Hormones are produced by endocrine glands, travel in the blood plasma and act on target organs.

questions.content: Which gland is known as the 'master gland'?
questions.explanation: The pituitary gland, at the base of the brain, releases hormones that control other glands.

questions.content: Which organ produces insulin?
questions.explanation: Insulin is made by the pancreas and lowers blood glucose concentration.

questions.content: What is homeostasis?
options: Keeping the internal environment of the body stable
questions.explanation: Homeostasis keeps conditions such as temperature, water and glucose level within narrow limits so cells work well.

questions.content: What is the normal core body temperature in humans?
questions.explanation: Human enzymes work best at about 37 °C.

questions.content: Which hormone prepares the body for 'fight or flight'?
questions.explanation: Adrenaline from the adrenal glands increases heart rate and breathing rate and sends more glucose to muscles.

questions.content: After a large meal, blood glucose rises. What happens next?
options: Insulin is released, and the liver converts glucose into glycogen
Glucagon is released and glycogen is converted into glucose
Adrenaline is released and glycogen is made
questions.explanation: Insulin causes cells and the liver to take up glucose and the liver stores it as glycogen, lowering blood glucose.

questions.content: This system of keeping a factor within limits by reversing a change is called...
questions.explanation: In negative feedback, a change in a variable triggers a response that brings it back towards the set point.

questions.content: Why do you shiver when your core temperature starts to fall?
options: Rapid muscle contractions release heat by respiration
questions.explanation: Shivering is a rapid muscle movement that increases respiration, so more heat is released to warm the body.

questions.content: On a hot day, which responses help to cool the body?
options: Shivering and narrowing of skin blood vessels
Sweating and narrowing of skin blood vessels
Sweating and widening of skin blood vessels (vasodilation)
questions.explanation: Sweat evaporates, taking heat from the skin, and wider vessels let more blood flow near the surface to lose heat.

questions.content: How does type 1 diabetes differ from type 2 diabetes?
options: In type 1 the pancreas does not make enough insulin; in type 2 cells respond poorly to insulin
Type 1 is caused by diet; type 2 is not
Type 2 has no effect on blood glucose
questions.explanation: Type 1 is usually treated with insulin injections. Type 2 is linked to lifestyle and is managed by diet, exercise and sometimes medication.

questions.content: Why are hormones slower to act than nerve impulses but often longer lasting?
options: They only act on the brain
They travel in the blood and remain active for a while
questions.explanation: Blood transport takes longer than electrical impulses, and hormones can last for minutes to hours or longer.

questions.content: Which hormone raises blood glucose when it is too low?
questions.explanation: Glucagon from the pancreas causes the liver to convert glycogen into glucose and release it into the blood.

questions.content: A person's blood glucose is measured every hour after a meal at 10:00. Results (mmol/dm³): 10:00 5.0, 11:00 8.0, 12:00 6.0, 13:00 5.0. What explains the fall between 11:00 and 13:00?
options: Glucagon released by the pancreas reduced blood glucose
Adrenaline released by the pancreas reduced blood glucose
Blood glucose fell because no food was eaten
Insulin released by the pancreas reduced blood glucose
questions.explanation: After the rise, negative feedback via insulin returned the level to about 5.0 mmol/dm³.

questions.content: A diabetic person injects too much insulin and feels shaky and confused. What is the most likely cause?
options: Blood glucose has fallen too low
Blood glucose has risen too high
questions.explanation: Too much insulin removes too much glucose from the blood, so cells such as brain cells get too little.

questions.content: Which description best explains why a thermostat is a good model of body temperature control?
options: A sensor detects a change and triggers a response that reverses it
questions.explanation: A thermostat and body temperature control both detect changes and switch on responses that return the value to the set point.

questions.content: A student claims: 'Negative feedback means a bad outcome.' How would you evaluate this?
options: Correct; negative feedback damages the body
Wrong; 'negative' means the response reverses the change, keeping conditions stable
Correct; it only happens in disease
Wrong; it makes the change bigger
questions.explanation: Negative feedback is beneficial, because it keeps variables near their set point. Positive feedback increases the change.

questions.content: Thyroxine from the thyroid gland controls metabolic rate. A patient has an underactive thyroid. Which set of symptoms is most likely?
options: Weight loss, sweating and feeling hot
Tiredness, weight gain and feeling cold
questions.explanation: Low thyroxine slows metabolic rate, so less energy is released: tiredness, weight gain and sensitivity to cold.

note:
Hormones and the endocrine system
The endocrine system is a set of glands that release **hormones** straight into the bloodstream. A hormone is a chemical messenger. It travels all around the body in the blood plasma, but only affects its **target organs**, which have the right receptors. Compared with the nervous system, hormones act more slowly but their effects usually last longer.

## Main glands and hormones
- **Pituitary gland** (base of the brain): the "master gland" that makes hormones that control other glands, and others such as growth hormone.
- **Thyroid gland** (neck): thyroxine, which controls the metabolic rate.
- **Adrenal glands** (above the kidneys): adrenaline, which prepares the body for "fight or flight" by increasing heart rate, breathing rate and blood glucose.
- **Pancreas**: insulin and glucagon, which control blood glucose.
- **Ovaries**: oestrogen. **Testes**: testosterone. These are sex hormones.

## Homeostasis
**Homeostasis** is the maintenance of a stable internal environment. Body temperature, blood glucose, water content and carbon dioxide levels are all controlled. If conditions drift too far, enzymes and cells stop working properly. Most of this uses **negative feedback**: a receptor detects a change away from the set point, a control centre processes it, and an effector produces a response that reverses the change.

## Controlling blood glucose
- After a meal, blood glucose rises. The pancreas releases **insulin**. Insulin makes liver and muscle cells take up glucose and the liver converts excess glucose into **glycogen** for storage. Blood glucose falls.
- Between meals or during exercise, blood glucose falls. The pancreas releases **glucagon**. Glucagon makes the liver convert glycogen back into glucose and release it into the blood. Blood glucose rises.

In **type 1 diabetes**, the pancreas does not make enough insulin, so blood glucose can get too high. It is controlled by insulin injections, healthy eating and monitoring. In **type 2 diabetes**, body cells respond less well to insulin. It is linked to obesity and low activity and is controlled by diet, exercise and sometimes drugs. Too much insulin can lower glucose too far, which causes shakiness and confusion.

## Controlling body temperature
The brain monitors the temperature of the blood and the skin has temperature receptors. The set point is about 37 °C.
- **Too hot**: sweat glands release sweat, which evaporates and cools the skin; blood vessels near the skin widen (vasodilation) so more heat is lost.
- **Too cold**: you shiver, so muscle contractions release heat; blood vessels near the skin narrow (vasoconstriction) so less heat is lost; hairs stand on end to trap an insulating layer of air.

## Nerves compared with hormones
Nervous responses are very fast, short-lived and act on a precise target. Hormonal responses are slower, longer-lasting and may affect many organs.

## Common mistakes
- Saying that insulin raises blood glucose. It lowers it.
- Confusing glucose and glycogen. Glucose is the sugar in blood; glycogen is the storage carbohydrate.
- Saying that blood vessels "move closer to the skin" instead of widening or narrowing.
- Thinking negative feedback is bad. It keeps things stable.

## How this is examined
Expect graphs of blood glucose after a meal, diagrams of feedback loops and questions about diabetes. You may need to describe a pattern, explain it using insulin and glucagon, and evaluate treatments.

Exam tip: For any homeostasis question, name the stimulus (change), the receptor, the effector response and show how the response reverses the change.

questions.content: Which is NOT a function of the skeleton?
questions.explanation: The skeleton supports the body, protects organs, allows movement with muscles and makes blood cells in bone marrow. Digestion is done by the digestive system.

questions.content: Which part of the skeleton protects the brain?
questions.explanation: The skull (cranium) surrounds and protects the brain. The ribcage protects the heart and lungs.

questions.content: What joins muscles to bones?
questions.explanation: Tendons attach muscle to bone. Ligaments attach bone to bone.

questions.content: Which type of joint is the elbow?
questions.explanation: The elbow and knee are hinge joints that move mainly in one plane, like a door.

questions.content: What happens to a muscle when it contracts?
questions.explanation: Muscles can only pull by contracting. They cannot push.

questions.content: Why are muscles arranged in antagonistic pairs?
options: Each muscle works twice as hard
One muscle pushes and the other pulls
Muscles can only pull, so one muscle is needed for each direction of movement
questions.explanation: For example, when the biceps contracts, the triceps relaxes to bend the arm, and the reverse to straighten it.

questions.content: When you straighten your arm, which muscle contracts?
questions.explanation: The triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes to extend the arm.

questions.content: What is the function of ligaments?
options: To hold bones together at a joint
To cushion the ends of bones
questions.explanation: Ligaments are strong, slightly elastic fibres that join bone to bone and stabilise the joint.

questions.content: Which feature of a synovial joint reduces friction?
questions.explanation: Cartilage covers the ends of bones and synovial fluid lubricates the joint, allowing smooth movement.

questions.content: Where in the skeleton are red blood cells made?
questions.explanation: Red blood cells, and most white blood cells, are made in the bone marrow of some bones such as the ribs and pelvis.

questions.content: Which joint allows movement in all directions, such as the shoulder?
questions.explanation: A ball and socket joint allows rotation and movement in many directions. The hip is another example.

questions.content: Why do muscle cells contain many mitochondria?
options: They need a lot of energy from aerobic respiration
questions.explanation: Contraction needs a lot of energy, which is released by aerobic respiration in mitochondria.

questions.content: Which nutrient pair is most important for strong bones?
questions.explanation: Calcium makes bones hard, and vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium.

questions.content: A person lifts a heavy box. The forearm is the lever, the elbow is the pivot and the biceps pulls on the forearm close to the elbow. What is the benefit of this arrangement?
options: The hand moves a small distance with a large force
The force on the hand is greater than the force in the biceps
A small contraction of the biceps moves the hand through a large distance
questions.explanation: The muscle attaches close to the pivot, so a small shortening moves the hand a long way. The trade-off is that the muscle must exert a larger force than the load.

questions.content: A physiotherapist explains that an injury that stretches a ligament in the knee can cause the knee to become unstable. Why?
options: Ligaments hold the bones together at the joint
Ligaments contract to move the leg
questions.explanation: A stretched or torn ligament no longer holds the bones firmly, so the joint moves in abnormal ways.

questions.content: Osteoporosis makes bones thinner and weaker. Which action is most likely to reduce the risk?
options: Weight-bearing exercise and calcium in the diet
questions.explanation: Weight-bearing exercise stimulates bone to build more strongly and calcium is required to make bone tissue.

questions.content: During a long run, a muscle cell has a lot of lactic acid. The person rests. Which explains the aching muscle?
options: Anaerobic respiration made lactic acid when oxygen supply was too low
The muscle ran out of bone
questions.explanation: When oxygen cannot be delivered quickly enough, muscle cells respire anaerobically, producing lactic acid. This builds up and causes fatigue.

questions.content: In an investigation, grip strength is measured for 30 students before and after four weeks of hand-exercise. The mean rises from 28.0 kg to 31.5 kg. What is the percentage increase?

note:
The skeletal and muscular systems
The skeleton and muscles work together as the body's frame and engine. They support you, protect delicate organs and let you move. Understanding how they cooperate also explains common injuries and why exercise and diet matter for bone and muscle health.

## Functions of the skeleton
- **Support**: the skeleton gives the body its shape and holds up soft tissues.
- **Protection**: the skull protects the brain, the ribcage protects the heart and lungs, and the backbone (vertebral column) protects the spinal cord.
- **Movement**: bones act as levers, and muscles pull on them.
- **Making blood cells**: red blood cells and many white blood cells are made in the bone marrow.
- **Storage**: bones store minerals such as calcium and phosphate.

Bone is living tissue with a blood supply. It is hard because of calcium minerals, with some flexible protein fibres. Cartilage is a softer, more flexible tissue found at the ends of bones, in the nose and ears, and as discs between vertebrae.

## Joints
A joint is where two or more bones meet.
- **Ball and socket joints** (hip, shoulder): movement in many directions.
- **Hinge joints** (elbow, knee): movement mostly back and forth in one plane.
- **Fixed joints** (skull): no movement, which protects the brain.

In a freely moving (synovial) joint, the ends of the bones are covered with smooth **cartilage**, which reduces friction and absorbs shock. **Synovial fluid** lubricates the joint. **Ligaments** join bone to bone and hold the joint in place. **Tendons** join muscle to bone.

## Muscles and movement
Muscles can only do one thing: contract (get shorter) and pull. They cannot push. This is why they work in **antagonistic pairs**, two muscles that act in opposite directions.
- To bend the arm (flexion), the biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes.
- To straighten it (extension), the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes.

The tendon of the biceps is attached to the forearm very close to the elbow. This arrangement means a short contraction produces a large movement of the hand, though the muscle has to exert more force than the weight lifted.

Muscle cells contain many mitochondria, because contracting needs a lot of energy from aerobic respiration. During intense exercise the oxygen supply may not keep up. The muscles then respire anaerobically and make lactic acid, which causes tiredness and aches.

## Keeping bones and muscles healthy
- A diet with calcium (dairy, leafy vegetables) and vitamin D (sunlight, oily fish) builds strong bones. Protein is needed to build and repair muscle.
- Weight-bearing exercise such as walking, running and sport makes bones stronger and muscles bigger.
- **Osteoporosis** is a condition where bones become thin and brittle, more common in older people. Exercise and calcium in the diet during life reduce the risk.
- Warming up and stretching reduce the risk of sprains (stretched or torn ligaments) and strains (torn muscles or tendons).

## Investigating muscle fitness
Typical investigations measure grip strength, how many repetitions someone can do or recovery time of heart rate. Good practice: use the same equipment, test several people, repeat and calculate a mean. To find a percentage change, use (new − old) ÷ old × 100. For example, grip strength rising from 28.0 kg to 31.5 kg is an increase of 12.5%.

## Common mistakes
- Mixing up tendons and ligaments. A helpful phrase: tendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone.
- Saying muscles push. They only pull.
- Saying the biceps and triceps contract together.
- Forgetting that bones are living and can grow and repair.

## How this is examined
Look for diagrams of the arm or knee, data from fitness tests, and questions about diet or injuries. Marks are gained for linking each structure to its function and explaining antagonistic action.

Exam tip: When explaining arm movement, name both muscles and state which contracts and which relaxes, for each direction.
